title: Managed Patch Management: Best Practices, SLAs, and How to Choose an MSP
author: SecureTrust Cyber
dek: How managed patch management works, which SLAs to demand, and how to choose an MSP, with a healthcare focus on HIPAA risk.
body:
Unpatched software remains one of the most reliable ways into a network. Attackers do not need clever zero-days when a known flaw sits unfixed on an exposed server for months. For healthcare organizations, where a single compromised system can disrupt patient care and trigger HIPAA exposure, patching is not housekeeping. It is a core control.

The problem is rarely that teams do not know patching matters. It is that patching is relentless, risky to get wrong, and easy to push down the priority list. That is why many organizations hand it to a managed service provider (MSP). This guide explains what managed patch management actually includes, the best practices that separate good programs from checkbox ones, the SLAs worth demanding, and how to evaluate a provider.

What Is Managed Patch Management?

Managed patch management is a service in which an external provider takes responsibility for identifying, testing, deploying, and verifying software updates across your environment. That typically covers operating systems, third-party applications, firmware, and sometimes network devices and cloud workloads.

A mature service is more than "turning on automatic updates." It includes:

  • Asset discovery and inventory so you know what needs patching in the first place
  • Vulnerability intelligence to decide which patches matter most right now
  • Testing and staged rollout to avoid breaking clinical or business systems
  • Deployment within agreed timelines
  • Verification and reporting proving the patch landed and the vulnerability is closed
  • Exception handling for systems that cannot be patched on schedule

Why Patching Fails in Practice

Most patching failures follow a few predictable patterns:

  1. Incomplete inventory. You cannot patch what you do not know exists. Shadow IT, forgotten servers, and unmanaged medical devices are common blind spots.
  2. Fear of downtime. Teams delay patches because a bad update could take down a critical system.
  3. Everything is "urgent." Without risk-based prioritization, teams chase every advisory and fall behind on the ones that matter.
  4. Third-party blind spots. Operating system patches are often handled, while browsers, PDF readers, remote access tools, and line-of-business software are missed.
  5. No verification. A deployment job reporting "success" is not the same as a vulnerability being remediated.

A good managed provider is built specifically to solve these problems.

Patch Management Best Practices

1. Start with a complete, living asset inventory

Patch coverage can never exceed inventory coverage. Combine agent-based discovery, network scanning, and cloud API data, and reconcile them regularly. Track the owner, business function, criticality, and exposure (internet-facing or internal) of each asset.

2. Prioritize by real-world risk, not just severity scores

CVSS scores are a starting point, not an answer. Better programs weigh:

  • Whether the vulnerability is known to be exploited in the wild (the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog is a practical source)
  • Whether the asset is internet-facing
  • The business and clinical criticality of the system
  • The presence of compensating controls such as segmentation or virtual patching

A medium-severity flaw on an exposed system with active exploitation can be more urgent than a critical-rated flaw on an isolated internal machine.

3. Test before you deploy broadly

Use a pilot group that represents your real environment, including at least one of each critical system type. For clinical and line-of-business applications, confirm vendor compatibility before rolling out. Staged rings (pilot, then early adopters, then general population) reduce the blast radius of a bad patch.

4. Define maintenance windows and rollback plans

Agree in advance when systems may reboot, who approves emergency changes, and how a failed patch is reversed. Healthcare environments in particular need windows that respect clinic hours and on-call coverage.

5. Cover third-party software and firmware

Operating system patching is the easy part. Include browsers, runtimes, remote access and VPN tools, hypervisors, firewalls, and endpoint agents. Many high-profile breaches have started with an unpatched edge device or a forgotten application, not a Windows update.

6. Verify with a rescan

After deployment, rescan to confirm the vulnerability no longer appears. Report on remediated findings, not just deployed patches.

7. Handle exceptions deliberately

Some systems cannot be patched quickly: legacy applications, vendor-locked medical devices, or systems awaiting a certified update. Document each exception with an owner, a business justification, an expiry date, and compensating controls such as network isolation, restricted access, or additional monitoring. Exceptions without expiry dates become permanent risk.

8. Measure what matters

Track metrics that show real exposure reduction (see the KPI section below), and review them with leadership regularly.

Patch Management SLAs: What to Demand

A service level agreement turns "we'll patch things" into an enforceable commitment. The exact numbers depend on your risk tolerance and environment, but the structure below is a widely used starting point.

Severity / Condition Typical Remediation Target
Emergency (actively exploited, internet-facing) 24 to 72 hours, often with mitigation sooner
Critical 7 days or less
High 14 to 30 days
Medium 30 to 60 days
Low 90 days or next maintenance cycle

These are illustrative targets, not regulatory mandates. Adjust them to your environment and risk appetite.

What a strong patching SLA includes

  • Clear severity definitions. Who decides what counts as "critical," and based on what inputs (CVSS, exploitation status, asset exposure)?
  • When the clock starts. From vendor release, from provider validation, or from your approval? This single detail changes the meaning of every number.
  • Coverage scope. Which operating systems, applications, firmware, and device types are included, and which are explicitly excluded?
  • Success criteria. Is a patch "done" when it is deployed, or when a rescan confirms remediation?
  • Exception process and timelines. How quickly are exceptions escalated, and who signs off?
  • Reporting cadence. Monthly at minimum, with real-time visibility into current exposure.
  • Remedies. What happens when targets are missed, such as service credits, root cause review, or escalation?

Be wary of SLAs measured only as a percentage of "patches deployed." A provider can hit 98% while the two systems that matter most remain exposed.

Healthcare Considerations

Healthcare environments add constraints that generic IT patching programs often ignore.

  • HIPAA Security Rule. The Security Rule requires covered entities and business associates to implement risk analysis and risk management processes. Known, unremediated vulnerabilities are difficult to defend in a risk analysis or after an incident.
  • Medical and IoT devices. Many devices run embedded or legacy operating systems and cannot be patched on the normal cycle. These need inventory, segmentation, and vendor coordination rather than standard automated deployment.
  • Clinical uptime. Maintenance windows must account for patient care, imaging, scheduling, and billing workflows.
  • Small practices and limited staff. Dental practices, specialty clinics, and small groups often have no dedicated security staff, which makes a managed approach especially valuable.

When evaluating a provider, ask directly whether they have experience with healthcare environments and with your specific practice management or EHR software.

How to Choose a Patch Management MSP

Use this checklist when comparing providers.

Scope and capability - Do they cover operating systems, third-party applications, firmware, and network devices? - Can they patch on-premises, remote, and cloud workloads? - How do they handle assets that cannot be patched?

Process and risk handling - Do they prioritize using exploitation data and asset context, or only CVSS? - What is their testing and staged-rollout process? - What is the rollback procedure when a patch breaks something?

Transparency and reporting - Can you see current patch status and open vulnerabilities in real time? - Do reports show remediation verified by rescan? - Will you receive evidence suitable for HIPAA risk analysis, cyber insurance questionnaires, and audits?

Contract and accountability - Are SLAs written with clear severity definitions and clock-start rules? - What are the remedies for missed targets? - Who owns the tooling and data if you leave?

Fit - Do they understand healthcare, or will you be teaching them your environment? - Will they integrate with your existing vulnerability scanning, SIEM, or endpoint tools? - Can they show references from organizations of similar size and complexity?

Red flags

  • Vague promises such as "we handle all patching" with no defined scope
  • SLAs that measure activity (patches sent) instead of outcomes (vulnerabilities closed)
  • No process for exceptions or unpatchable assets
  • Reporting limited to a monthly PDF with no verification
  • Reluctance to explain how they prioritize

KPIs to Track

Whatever provider you choose, hold the program to a short set of measurable indicators:

  • Patch coverage: percentage of in-scope assets actually under management
  • Mean time to remediate (MTTR) by severity
  • SLA compliance rate by severity, not just overall
  • Exposure window for actively exploited vulnerabilities
  • Open exceptions and how many are past their expiry date
  • Failed or rolled-back deployments
  • Reboot-pending systems that are patched in name only

Building a Patching Program That Holds Up

If you are starting from scratch or rebuilding, a practical sequence looks like this:

  1. Inventory first. Establish what you have and who owns it.
  2. Define severity and SLA tiers with leadership agreement.
  3. Pilot with a representative group, then expand in rings.
  4. Automate the routine and reserve human review for exceptions and emergencies.
  5. Verify with rescans and report remediation, not activity.
  6. Review quarterly and adjust targets as your environment and threat picture change.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between patch management and vulnerability management?

Vulnerability management finds and prioritizes weaknesses. Patch management is one of the primary ways those weaknesses get fixed. A strong program connects the two so that scan findings drive patch priorities and rescans confirm the result.

How fast should critical vulnerabilities be patched?

Many organizations target seven days or less for critical findings, and 24 to 72 hours for actively exploited, internet-facing systems. If a patch cannot be applied in that window, apply compensating controls and document the exception.

Does managed patching replace my internal IT team?

Usually not. It takes over the repetitive, time-sensitive work while your team retains decisions about risk, business priorities, and exceptions. The best arrangements are a partnership with clear roles.

Can small practices benefit from managed patch management?

Yes. Small organizations are often the least resourced and still face the same automated attacks as large ones. A managed service gives them consistent coverage and documentation without needing a full-time security hire.

What about systems that cannot be patched?

Isolate them on a segmented network, restrict who and what can reach them, monitor them closely, and track a documented exception with an owner and an expiry date. Plan for replacement or vendor-supported upgrade.

The Bottom Line

Effective patching is not about installing every update the moment it appears. It is about knowing your assets, prioritizing by real risk, deploying safely, and proving the vulnerability is gone. The right managed partner makes that process consistent and measurable, and writes it into an SLA you can hold them to.

If you are weighing whether to bring patching in-house or hand it to a provider, start with your inventory and the SLA table above. Those two documents will tell you quickly where you stand and what to ask for.
